question: A square is easy to cut into 2, 4, 6 — any even number — of triangles of equal area. Into how many triangles of equal area can a square be cut if the number must be odd?
choices: Any odd number of three or more works
No odd number is possible at all
Only odd numbers that are perfect squares
Only odd numbers above a certain minimum size
anchorText: it is not possible to dissect a square into an odd number of triangles of equal area

question: 'Squaring the circle' is the byword for an impossible task. Yet it has been mathematically proven that you CAN cut a disk into finitely many pieces and rearrange them into a square of exactly equal area.
choices: True
False
anchorText: It is possible, using pieces that are Borel sets

question: The sum of the reciprocals of all the prime numbers (1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + ...) grows forever without bound. The same is true if you add up the reciprocals of only the twin primes.
choices: True
False
anchorText: the sum of the reciprocals of the twin primes converges to a finite value

question: Arrange 12 equal balls so each touches a central ball of the same size and you'll see sizeable gaps left over. Can a 13th be squeezed in to touch the center too?
choices: Yes — there is clearly room for one more
No — twelve is the proven maximum
anchorText: Newton correctly thought that the limit was 12; Gregory thought that a 13th could fit

question: There is a function that is continuous (no jumps) everywhere and has a slope of exactly zero at almost every single point — and yet it still climbs steadily from 0 up to 1.
choices: True
False
anchorText: continuous everywhere and has zero derivative almost everywhere

question: To stop otherwise-uncontrollable epileptic seizures in a child, neurosurgeons sometimes resort to doing what?
choices: Removing or disconnecting an entire half of the brain
Cutting the nerve pathways to both ears
Replacing part of the skull with a metal plate
Removing both of the temporal lobes
anchorText: an unhealthy hemisphere of the brain is disconnected or removed

question: Competitive breath-hold divers are warned never to hyperventilate (take rapid deep breaths) right before going under. Why is that dangerous?
choices: The forceful breathing can rupture delicate lung tissue
It delays the urge to breathe, so a diver can black out from low oxygen without warning
It loads the blood with so much oxygen that it turns toxic
It brings on a painful squeeze in the sinuses and ears on the way down
anchorText: hypoxia expedited by hypocapnia caused by voluntary hyperventilation before the dive

question: Given a perfect supply of nutrients in a lab dish, how many times can a normal human body cell divide before division stops for good?
choices: Indefinitely — with nutrients, normal cells are effectively immortal
About 40 to 60 times, then it stops
Exactly once, and then it dies
Several thousand times
anchorText: will divide between 40 and 60 times in cell culture before entering a senescence phase

question: People with severe, long-standing dementia sometimes unexpectedly regain clear memory and recognition of loved ones in the days or hours just before they die.
choices: True
False
anchorText: an unexpected return of mental clarity shortly before death
